nameStory: Spotted St. John's wort gets its name from the tiny dark spots scattered across its bright yellow petals, like freckles on a sunny face. The "St. John's wort" part comes from the tradition of gathering these golden flowers around St. John's Day (June 24th), when many species in this family reach peak bloom.
description: Spotted St. John's wort is a cheerful perennial wildflower that brightens New England meadows and roadsides with clusters of small, bright yellow flowers. This native herb typically grows 1-3 feet tall with an upright, branching stem. The five-petaled flowers are sprinkled with distinctive dark spots or dots, making them look like tiny golden suns with beauty marks.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with five petals marked by small dark spots or lines, especially along the petal edges. Each flower is about half an inch across and feels delicate to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite leaves (growing in pairs across from each other) that are oval-shaped with smooth edges. Hold a leaf up to the light to see tiny translucent dots scattered throughout.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright plant reaching 1-3 feet tall with multiple branching stems. Often grows in small colonies, spreading by underground runners.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small reddish-brown capsules that split open to release tiny seeds. The dried seed pods often persist into fall, rattling softly when shaken.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, somewhat square stems that feel firm but not woody. When crushed, the plant may release a faint, slightly resinous scent.

habitat: Look for spotted St. John's wort in sunny, open areas like meadows, old fields, roadsides, and woodland edges throughout New England. It prefers well-drained soils and doesn't mind poor or disturbed ground. You'll often find it growing alongside goldenrod, asters, and other common wildflowers in areas that get plenty of sunlight.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge in late spring with fresh green opposite leaves. The plant forms bushy clumps as stems branch and grow taller.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time from June through August, when clusters of spotted yellow flowers create bright displays. This is the best time for positive identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and small seed capsules develop, turning reddish-brown. Leaves may yellow slightly but often stay green well into fall.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back, leaving dried brown stems with persistent seed capsules that may rattle in winter winds.

funFact: The leaves contain hypericin, a compound that's toxic to grazing mammals but harmless to the insects that love visiting the flowers - it's like the plant has a built-in security system that protects it from being eaten while still welcoming helpful pollinators!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with common St. John's wort, but spotted St. John's wort has obvious dark spots on its petals while common St. John's wort has clear yellow petals with black dots only along the edges. Memory trick: "Spotted has spots, common keeps it clean."
contextualKnowledge: St. John's wort plants have been used medicinally for centuries, though spotted St. John's wort is less commonly used than its European cousin, common St. John's wort. Despite their medicinal reputation, these plants can cause photosensitivity in livestock, making animals more susceptible to sunburn.
compareHints: Among New England's St. John's worts, spotted St. John's wort is medium-sized and easily distinguished by its clearly spotted petals. Common St. John's wort has unspotted yellow petals, while smaller relatives like dwarf St. John's wort have tiny flowers without prominent spots. The translucent dots in the leaves (visible when held to light) are found in most St. John's worts, but the petal spots make this species unmistakable.
